question: A new study by the Technical University of Munich (TUM) has exposed major flaws in how the EU regulates CO2 emissions from passenger cars1. The core problem is that EU rules focus on tailpipe emissions, rather than considering a vehicle’s entire life cycle.

Led by professors Johannes Fottner, Magnus Fröhling and Tim Büthe, the study analysed vehicles’ climate footprints across their life cycle, from production and use to disposal, which the Commission’s current approach does not account for. It found that the life cycle CO2 emissions of battery-electric vehicles are, on average, only 41 % lower than those of combustion engine vehicles.
Yet EU rules treat them as ‘zeroemission’. This miscalculation could have adverse economic and environmental consequences. 1.
Is the Commission aware of this study, and if so, does it intend to address the flaws the study underlines in the current EU regulatory approach?
Will the Commission now revise how emissions targets and penalties are calculated to take account of emissions throughout a vehicle’s entire life cycle?
If so, does the Commission intend to amend Regulation (EU) 2019/6312 to mandate verified life cycle emissions reporting for passenger cars?
